traveler: Saint Blaise of Sebastea (Blasius, Sveti Vlaho, San Biagio)
title: The Cave, the Comb and the Crossed Candles: Blaise of Sebastea, from Lesser Armenia to Ragusa and Maratea
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Sebastea, birth in Lesser Armenia
stops.date_confidence: unrecorded. No source gives a birth year: the legendary Acts give none, Wikipedia's infobox leaves the field empty, and the Catholic Encyclopedia calls every particular of his life legendary. 280 is a placeholder, not a datum.
stops.campa: In Sebastea, the walled capital of Lesser Armenia where the roads out of the uplands meet, a son is born to a wealthy and noble house. They name him Blasius, Blaise. The city is Roman by administration, Armenian by blood, and Christian in a quarter of its streets; it will make bishops and burn them inside the same century. Nothing of the birth is written down at the time. Everything known of it comes from Acts composed some four hundred years later, in another language, for readers who wanted a saint and were given one.
suggested_refs: The site of ancient Sebastea beneath modern Sivas, Turkey
sources: Legendary Acts of St Blaise, summarized at theeasternchurch.com and maryourhelp.org

stops.name: Sebastea, the physician who takes no fee
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The Acts alone; no independent attestation of the medical training or the practice.
stops.campa: He studies philosophy first, then medicine, and practices it in his own city without charging for it. The Greek church files such men under a standing category, the anargyroi, the unmercenaries: physicians who treat the body for nothing and the soul on the same visit. Animals are brought to him as readily as people, and he treats them too. Everything later attached to his name runs back through that one habit, the healing of whatever arrives at the door, the sore throats of Europe as much as the cattle of Cornish farmers.
suggested_refs: The Orthodox class of the anargyroi, the unmercenary physician saints

stops.name: Sebastea, chosen bishop by acclamation
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Sebastea's standing as an episcopal see is attested; the manner and year of his election are not, and rest on the Acts.
stops.campa: The bishop of Sebastea dies and the city puts its physician in his place by acclamation, without a synod having to be persuaded. He is consecrated over a see at the eastern hinge of the empire, where the roads from Caesarea, Nicopolis and Armenia Interior come together. A doctor becomes a bishop and does not stop being a doctor. The see itself is the hard fact in the whole dossier: the city existed, it had bishops, and no church has ever venerated a different bishop of Sebastea for these years.
suggested_refs: The episcopal list of Sebastea in Lesser Armenia

stops.name: Vagharshapat, Armenia comes to the font
stops.date_confidence: traditional date for Armenia's conversion. No source connects Blaise to Gregory the Illuminator or to King Tiridates, and the atlas carries no traveler for either. This is a gap, recorded as a gap, not a crossing.
stops.campa: Two hundred miles east, at Vagharshapat, Gregory the Illuminator brings King Tiridates to the font and Armenia becomes the first kingdom to take Christianity as its own. Blaise's Lesser Armenia lies on the Roman side of that frontier and receives no royal protection; it gets the imperial calendar of edicts instead. Within fifteen years the kingdom that converted its king will be watching the empire behead an Armenian bishop for refusing incense. The two facts sit a fortnight's ride apart and no ancient writer puts them in one sentence.
suggested_refs: The cathedral of Etchmiadzin at Vagharshapat, foundation of Christian Armenia
sources: absence check across the atlas journey files for gregory_the_illuminator and tiridates

stops.name: Byzantium, the persecution already running
stops.date_confidence: attested for Acacius; the Great Persecution edict is posted at Nicomedia on 23 February 303. The linkage to Blaise is thematic, not documentary: he dies under a different emperor a decade later.
stops.campa: Thirteen years before Blaise is taken, the machinery is already turning at the other end of the same empire. Acacius, a Cappadocian centurion, is scourged and beheaded at Byzantium; Vitus dies a boy at Rome; Barbara is killed at Heliopolis under the columns of Baalbek. Their journeys are already in the atlas and their deaths belong to Diocletian, not to Licinius. Blaise will die a decade later, under another emperor, in another province, and in fourteen hundred years all four will be prayed to in one breath from the same German altar.
suggested_refs: The Diocletianic edict posted at Nicomedia, 23 February 303

stops.name: Nicomedia, the rescript of toleration
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Licinian rescript settling toleration is published at Nicomedia in June 313.
stops.campa: Licinius publishes at Nicomedia the settlement agreed with Constantine at Milan: Christians may worship, and confiscated property goes back to them. Constantine's own journey pins this city twice, once for the rescript and once, eleven years later, for the hunting down of the man who published it. At Sebastea the parchment changes nothing the governor does not want changed. Toleration is an imperial document; persecution is a provincial habit. The Acts of Blaise open their real action after the edict, not before it, which is their strangest feature.
suggested_refs: The Licinian rescript of toleration, published at Nicomedia, June 313

stops.name: The mountain above Sebastea, the hermitage
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The Golden Legend places him in an unnamed hermitage in a ditch, fed by birds; the Acts summaries say only a cavern. No source names the mountain, so the coordinates here are simply Sebastea's.
stops.campa: With the edict published and the province unchanged, the bishop leaves the city and goes up onto the mountain to a cave. The Golden Legend says a hermitage in a ditch, and that the birds of heaven brought him meat there to eat. Nobody comes for him at first. He prays, he waits out the governor, and the wilderness above Sebastea keeps him the way it keeps wolves and shepherds, without asking after his office. The Acts do not say how long he stays. They rarely say how long about anything.
suggested_refs: The Golden Legend's unnamed hermitage in a ditch, fed by birds
sources: The Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine), Life of S. Blase, trans. Caxton

stops.name: The cave, the beasts come to be healed
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Golden Legend and the Acts; the episode has no independent trace and is the oldest of the purely hagiographic accretions.
stops.campa: Wild animals come down to the cave in herds and wait. They do him no harm; the sick and the injured among them stand to be handled, and he blesses them and heals them and they go. When he is at prayer they will not interrupt, and they wait for him to finish. It is the least defensible thing in his dossier and the one image the painters never abandoned: a bishop in a rock cleft with his hand on the flank of something that ought to have eaten him. The physician who charged nobody has stopped distinguishing between patients.
suggested_refs: The iconographic type of Blaise among the beasts, standard in Western painting
sources: The Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase

stops.name: Mount Argaeus, the mountain the later tellings name
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved here. The Argaeus identification appears only in late retellings; neither the Golden Legend nor the Acts summaries name it. Erciyes stands about 165 km from Sebastea, beside Caesarea, in another province. Pinned as a rival claim.
stops.campa: Later tellings give the cave an address: Mount Argaeus, the snow cone the Greeks called Argaios and the Turks call Erciyes, standing over Caesarea in Cappadocia. It is a magnificent mountain and it is the wrong one. It lies a hundred and sixty-five kilometres from his see, across a provincial boundary, beside a rival metropolitan city that had saints of its own and no need of his. The pin is set here anyway, because the tradition set it here, and because the atlas records where a story travelled as well as where it began.
suggested_refs: Mount Erciyes (ancient Argaeus) above Kayseri, the late gloss on the cave
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Blaise' (which does not name the mountain)

stops.name: The cave, the hunters of Agricolaus
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The Acta Sanctorum summaries name the governor Agricolaus and date the arrest to 316 under Licinius; the Catholic Encyclopedia rules the whole Acts dossier legendary, and Licinius is not documented persecuting Christians in 316.
stops.campa: Agricolaus, governor of Cappadocia and Lesser Armenia, orders a hunt, and the hunters come back having found no game and one bishop. They had been following the animals. The beasts standing quietly around a man in a cave are what betray him: the miracle and the arrest are a single event. He is brought down the mountain in chains, at the order of a governor serving an emperor who had put his name to a toleration rescript three years earlier and two provinces west.
suggested_refs: Agricolaus, governor of Cappadocia and Lesser Armenia in the Acta Sanctorum text
sources: Acta Sanctorum, cited in Wikipedia, 'Saint Blaise'

stops.name: A village near Sebastea, the widow's pig
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Golden Legend only; the village is unnamed and the coordinates are Sebastea's.
stops.campa: On the way down, a poor widow runs to him. A wolf has carried off her pig, which is the whole of her property with legs under it. Blaise tells her not to be angry, that she shall have her swine again, and the wolf brings it back to her alive and unhurt. She will see him once more, in prison, and she will not come empty-handed. Of all the wonders in his Acts this is the one that stays domestic. No emperor appears in it and nothing burns. A woman keeps her pig, and the debt she runs up will be paid back in wax.
stops.quote: Good woman anger thee not, for thou shalt have again thy swine
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine), Life of S. Blase, trans. William Caxton, ed. F.S. Ellis, 1900 (Fordham Medieval Sourcebook)
suggested_refs: The Caxton Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase, at the Fordham Medieval Sourcebook
sources: The Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase, trans. Caxton

stops.name: The road into Sebastea, the boy and the fishbone
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The founding episode of the throat patronage, known only from the Acts and their Latin descendants. Some tellings set it on the road, others in the prison; the sources are not reconciled.
stops.campa: Closer to the city a mother pushes through the guards and lays her son at the bishop's feet. The boy is choking on a fishbone and going blue. Blaise puts his hand on him and prays, not only for this child but for everyone who will ever ask health in his name, and the bone comes free. Every crossed candle held under a chin on the third of February for the next seventeen centuries issues from this one minute on a road in Armenia, with a prisoner's irons on the hands doing the healing.
stops.quote: And S. Blase put his hand upon him and made his prayer to God that this child, and all they that demanded benefits of health in his name, that they should be holpen and obtain it, and anon he was whole and guerished.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine), Life of S. Blase, trans. William Caxton, ed. F.S. Ellis, 1900 (Fordham Medieval Sourcebook)
suggested_refs: The Blessing of Throats in the Roman Ritual, derived from this episode
sources: The Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase, trans. Caxton

stops.name: Sebastea, the prison
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Golden Legend and the Acts; no cell, no prison building and no custodian is named anywhere.
stops.campa: They put him in a cell in his own episcopal city, to be held until the governor has time for him. He had been the physician here, and free of charge; the guards on the door will have known his face and some of them will have owed him. The Acts spend almost nothing on the cell itself. What they do record is the traffic through it, which tells you either that the prison was slack or that the city did not agree with the sentence coming. A widow gets in, and a mother with a choking boy gets close enough to lay him down at the bishop's feet.
suggested_refs: The prison scenes of the Passio, source of the candle motif
sources: The Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase, trans. Caxton

stops.name: The prison, the widow's two candles
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Golden Legend and the Feast of Saint Blaise tradition; the tie between the two candles and the Candlemas season is a later reading, not part of the Acts.
stops.campa: The widow whose pig came back kills it, and brings him the head and the feet, bread, and two wax candles for the dark of the cell. He thanks her and tells her to keep his day every year with a candle, and she will lack nothing. February is already the month of candles in the church's calendar; his feast falls the day after Candlemas. The wax that a widow carried into a prison in Armenia is still burning, crossed at the throat, in every parish that keeps the third of February.
suggested_refs: The two candles of the widow, ancestor of the crossed candles of the throat blessing
sources: The Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase, trans. Caxton

segments.name: The Tribunal of Agricolaus, and the Emperors Who Outlive Him

stops.name: Sebastea, before the governor
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The trial survives only in the Passio. Tag corrected from attested: citing the Acta Sanctorum for this scene does not make it documentary, and the Catholic Encyclopedia rules the dossier legendary.
stops.campa: Agricolaus offers the standard bargain of the century: a pinch of incense, a fixed formula, and the accused goes home. Blaise answers in the register the Acts keep for him throughout, which is less defiance than a flat refusal of the premise. He is the servant of God. He does not adore fiends. The governor has him beaten with staves and sent back to the cell, so the interview is adjourned rather than concluded, and in documents of this kind an adjournment always means the second hearing will use iron.
stops.quote: Poor caitiff, know thou that I am servant of God, and I adore not the fiends as ye do.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine), Life of S. Blase, trans. William Caxton, ed. F.S. Ellis, 1900 (Fordham Medieval Sourcebook)
suggested_refs: The tribunal formulary of the Passio: sacrifice, refusal, adjournment
sources: The Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase, trans. Caxton
Acta Sanctorum, cited in Wikipedia, 'Saint Blaise'

stops.name: Sebastea, the pillar and the iron combs
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The torture is Passio material. What is attested is the result: Blaise is patron of the wool combers and the comb is his fixed attribute. Wikipedia frames the causal link as conjecture, likely due to the similarity of the instruments.
stops.campa: At the second hearing they tie him to a pillar and tear his flesh with the iron combs used for carding wool. He tells the governor he has no dread of his menaces and delivers him his body whole. The instrument outlives the man. It goes into the panel paintings, the parish glass and the guild banners of wool towns from Bradford to Norwich, until a rake of iron teeth means Blaise the way keys mean Peter. The trade that adopted him did so because it recognised its own tool in the picture of his death.
stops.quote: Right cruel man I have no dread of thy menaces, do what thou wilt, I deliver to thee my body whole.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine), Life of S. Blase, trans. William Caxton, ed. F.S. Ellis, 1900 (Fordham Medieval Sourcebook)
suggested_refs: The iron wool comb as the standard iconographic attribute of Blaise
sources: The Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase, trans. Caxton
Louis Reau, Iconographie de l'art chretien

stops.name: A lake near Sebastea, the water that holds him
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Golden Legend; the lake is unnamed. The Caxton text gives sixty-five drowned, and retellings that say seven have conflated them with the seven women.
stops.campa: The governor orders him drowned. Blaise makes the sign of the cross over the water, walks out onto it, sits down in the middle of the lake and invites the men on the bank to come and prove their own gods by doing the same. Sixty-five of them try it. The lake takes all sixty-five. Then an angel tells him to come ashore and receive the crown prepared for him, and he walks back to the men who are waiting to kill him, which is the only reason the story does not end here with a bishop sitting on water in an empty province.
suggested_refs: The lake episode of the Golden Legend, with sixty-five drowned
sources: The Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase, trans. Caxton

stops.name: Sebastea, the seven women who gather the blood
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Golden Legend, corroborated by OrthodoxWiki, which counts two children and seven women martyred with him in 316.
stops.campa: Seven women follow him through the streets, stooping to gather the drops of his blood off the stones. They are arrested for it and ordered to sacrifice, and they refuse, and they are killed. OrthodoxWiki keeps them in the record together with two children who die at the same time, so the Eastern calendar remembers not one martyr at Sebastea but ten. The Western tradition narrowed down to the bishop alone and gave him a comb and a candle. The seven kept only their number.
stops.quote: There were seven women that siewed him, which gathered up the drops of his blood, which women anon were taken, and constrained to sacrifice to their gods.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine), Life of S. Blase, trans. William Caxton, ed. F.S. Ellis, 1900 (Fordham Medieval Sourcebook)
suggested_refs: The seven women and two children of Sebastea in the Eastern synaxaria
sources: The Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase, trans. Caxton

stops.name: Sebastea, the beheading
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Most accounts place the martyrdom under Licinius about 316; no source records the day. 3 February is the Western feast, not a date of death, and the 283 variant that circulates is uncorroborated in anything reachable.
stops.campa: He is beheaded with the two children, by order of Agricolaus, in the city where he had been physician and bishop. Before the stroke he prays for the same thing he prayed for on the road: that whoever asks his help against the infirmity of the throat, or against any other sickness, be heard. A voice answers that the petition is granted. The West keeps his day on the third of February and the East on the eleventh, and neither number is the day he died, because nobody wrote that down.
stops.quote: And anon then the tyrant did do smite off his head, and S. Blase prayed to our Lord tofore his death that whosoever desired his help from the infirmity of the throat, or required aid for any other sickness or infirmity, that he would hear him.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend (Jacobus de Voragine), Life of S. Blase, trans. William Caxton, ed. F.S. Ellis, 1900 (Fordham Medieval Sourcebook)
suggested_refs: The Roman Martyrology entry for 3 February; the Byzantine synaxarion for 11 February
sources: The Golden Legend, Life of S. Blase, trans. Caxton

stops.name: Sebastea, Elisa buries the body
stops.date_confidence: legendary, from theeasternchurch.com. Gap: no tomb of Blaise at Sebastea is documented or excavated, and every relic tradition begins with a translation rather than with a grave.
stops.campa: A woman named Elisa takes the body away in the night and buries it. That is the whole of the record. No grave has ever been located at Sivas, no shrine there is described by any pilgrim, no excavation has produced a martyrium under the modern city. Every later claim on his bones, Maratea's and Ragusa's alike, begins with a ship or a translation and never with an opened tomb. The cult of Blaise has relics in a dozen countries and an origin nowhere.
suggested_refs: The absent tomb of Sebastea, a stated gap in the hagiographic record
sources: absence of archaeological record for a Sebastea tomb

stops.name: Cibalae, the emperors fight for the world
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle, 8 October 316. Flagged strain: Licinius is at war with Constantine in Pannonia in the year the Acts have him persecuting in Armenia, and his documented anti-Christian measures fall around 320 to 324.
stops.campa: In the same year the Acts give for the beheading, Licinius is nine hundred miles west of Sebastea, losing a battle to Constantine on the Pannonian plain at Cibalae. The peace that follows hands him the East, and leaves Armenia, Pontus and Cappadocia inside his jurisdiction: on this reckoning Blaise dies inside the realm the losing emperor has just been confirmed in. Constantine's own journey through the atlas crosses this field. The two men never meet; what they share is a governor whose authority runs back to the same throne.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Cibalae in Pannonia, 8 October 316

stops.name: Chrysopolis, the end of the persecutor
stops.date_confidence: attested. Chrysopolis, 18 September 324; Licinius flees to Nicomedia and is taken there.
stops.campa: Eight years after Sebastea, Constantine crosses the straits and breaks Licinius at Chrysopolis, opposite Byzantium. Licinius runs for Nicomedia, the city where he had published the toleration rescript in 313, and is taken there and killed the following year. The emperor under whose authority a bishop of Sebastea was beheaded is finished within the same decade, in the same eastern half, on the losing side of the war that makes Christianity the religion of the state. Nothing in the record says anyone at Sebastea noticed.
suggested_refs: Chrysopolis (Uskudar), site of Licinius's final defeat

stops.name: Constantinople, the physician who writes his name down
stops.date_confidence: attested as the earliest datable reference to Blaise. Aetius of Amida practised in the earlier sixth century at the imperial court; the year of the passage itself is not fixed, and the pin is his place of work, not Amida.
stops.campa: The first datable trace of Blaise anywhere is not a shrine or a calendar entry but a prescription. Aetius of Amida, physician of the Byzantine court, writing his medical compendium, instructs the practitioner to invoke the aid of Saint Blaise when an object is lodged in a patient's throat. Two centuries after the beheading, and two centuries before the Acts are composed, the saint already exists inside the profession he practised, doing the one thing everybody remembers him for. All the rest of the dossier is later than this sentence.
suggested_refs: The medical compendium of Aetius of Amida, earliest datable mention of Blaise

stops.name: Constantinople, the East fixes the eleventh of February
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Byzantine cult is established by the sixth century; the precise year the feast enters the calendar is not recorded and 550 stands for the century.
stops.campa: By the sixth century he is venerated across the Byzantine church, kept on the eleventh of February, and classed among the hieromartyrs and the unmercenary physicians. The cult travels the way liturgies travel, out of the capital and through the provinces, and Cappadocia and Armenia keep him as a local son. He is still, at this point, an entirely eastern saint. No church in the Latin West carries his name, and no western group honours him at all. The Acts that will carry him there have not yet been written.
suggested_refs: The Byzantine synaxarion for 11 February

stops.name: Rome, the Acts arrive and the West takes him up
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Acts are written roughly 400 years after his death and that no group honours him in the West before the eighth century. The place of composition is unknown; the Rome pin stands for the Latin church, not for a manuscript.
stops.campa: About four hundred years after the beheading, someone writes the Acts: the cave, the beasts, the wolf, the fishbone, the combs, the lake and the sixty-five drowned. Everything the world knows about Blaise enters the record in this one document, from an author whose name and city are lost. In the same century the cult crosses into the Latin West, where no group had honoured him before, and it arrives with the whole legend already attached to it. The West never knew a Blaise without the story.
suggested_refs: The legendary Acts of St Blaise, composed c. 700, source of the entire narrative

stops.name: Sebastea, the relics put to sea
stops.date_confidence: tradition, local to Maratea and reported in Wikipedia's article on the town. No port, captain, route or documentary year exists; the flight from Leo III's iconoclasm is the tradition's own explanation of itself.
stops.campa: Under Leo the Isaurian, with imperial officers breaking images across the East, the bones are said to be taken out of Sebastea and put aboard a ship bound for Rome. The tradition never names the port, the captain or the road down to the coast. It names only the reason, which is that the East had become dangerous for the things Christians keep, and the direction, which is west. What is described as sailing is not a fragment but the whole of him. Sebastea, which has no documented grave to lose, loses him anyway.
suggested_refs: The iconoclast persecutions of Leo III the Isaurian, given as the cause of the translation
sources: local tradition, Basilica di San Biagio

stops.name: Maratea, the ship that goes no further
stops.date_confidence: tradition. Wikipedia's Maratea article carries the 732 arrival and the relics still kept in the basilica; the temple of Minerva beneath it is unproven, it.wikipedia noting that no evidence has been officially found.
stops.campa: The ship stops at Maratea on the Tyrrhenian coast of Lucania and goes no further. The relics come ashore and are carried up Monte San Biagio to the church on the summit, raised, the town says, over a temple of Minerva whose stones nobody has yet produced. He becomes the town's patron and the mountain takes his name. Every year on the second Sunday of May the silver statue comes down the hill in procession to the old town, and Maratea keeps a claim on him that Ragusa has never conceded.
suggested_refs: The Basilica di San Biagio on Monte San Biagio, Maratea

stops.name: Maratea, the manna and Pope Pius IV
stops.date_confidence: attested. it.wikipedia, Basilica di San Biagio (Maratea), gives 4 March 1562 for the indulgences and the recognition of the manna; the 1563 date in circulation is a year late.
stops.campa: On the fourth of March 1562 Pius the Fourth grants indulgences to the sanctuary and recognises what Maratea calls the miracle of the holy manna: a clear liquid the town says weeps from the relics in the chapel above the sea. The recognition is a legal act about a substance. What the town had asserted for itself for centuries now stands acknowledged at Rome, and from this year the basilica on the mountain is a destination and not only a parish church.
suggested_refs: The chapel of the Regia Cappella and the cult of the Santa Manna at Maratea

stops.name: Maratea, the royal chapel of Philip IV
stops.date_confidence: attested. Royal letter of 23 December 1629 placing the basilica under the tutela of the royal curia, per it.wikipedia. Circulating summaries misplace this chapel in Madrid; the chapel is at Maratea.
stops.campa: By letter of the twenty-third of December 1629, Philip the Fourth, as king of Naples, places the basilica of San Biagio under the protection of the royal curia and makes it a regia cappella. An Armenian bishop beheaded by a Roman governor is now, in law, under the personal guard of the Spanish crown, on a mountain in Basilicata, eleven hundred miles from his see. The Habsburgs are gone from Naples within eighty years. The title regia cappella is still the church's.
suggested_refs: The 1629 royal letter making San Biagio di Maratea a regia cappella

stops.name: Maratea, the cannonball that does not burst
stops.date_confidence: tradition, local to Maratea. The December 1806 French siege is historical; the unexploded shot and its preservation rest on the town's own account.
stops.campa: In December 1806, with French troops reducing the last Bourbon holdouts in Lucania, a shot strikes the basilica on the mountain and does not explode. The town keeps the ball. It is shown as evidence of the same protection that produced the manna and licensed the crown's guardianship, and it is the last item added to the Maratea dossier: a bishop who freed a throat in Armenia and stopped a cannonball in Basilicata, fifteen hundred years apart, entered on the same account.
suggested_refs: The preserved French cannonball at the basilica of Maratea

segments.name: Ragusa Takes Him for Its Own

stops.name: Dubrovnik, the vision of the priest Stojko
stops.date_confidence: civic tradition. Wikipedia's article on the Festivity of Saint Blaise dates the vision and the Venetian attempt to 972 and the continuous observance from that year; 971 circulates widely in local retellings and the two are not reconciled here.
stops.campa: A Venetian fleet lies off Ragusa taking on water, and says it is doing nothing else. Blaise appears by night to a priest named Stojko, an old man with a white beard, a mitre and a staff, and tells him the ships intend to take the city. Stojko carries the warning to the senate, the walls are manned, the fleet leaves. The republic takes him as its patron on the spot and has never taken another. Its coins, its banners, its gates and its state seal all show a bishop holding a model of the town in his hand.
suggested_refs: The church of Sveti Vlaho on the Stradun, Dubrovnik
sources: Wikipedia, 'Festivity of Saint Blaise, the patron of Dubrovnik'

stops.name: Dubrovnik, the treasury and the crowned skull
stops.date_confidence: attested for the treasury holdings and for the feast as an established civic tradition by 1190. The reliquaries date from the eleventh to the eighteenth centuries and the arrival date of the head is not recorded.
stops.campa: The cathedral treasury holds his skull in a case of gold shaped as a Byzantine imperial crown, jewelled and enamelled, and his arm and his leg in reliquaries of their own. The head is crowned because what Ragusa kept in that case was a sovereign rather than a bishop. By 1190 the feast of Sveti Vlaho is documented as the city's established civic rite. The relics are brought out and shown, the standards go up, and the republic renews itself each year around the bones of a man from a city it never traded with.
suggested_refs: The reliquary bust of Sveti Vlaho in the Dubrovnik cathedral treasury

stops.name: Dubrovnik, the third of February and UNESCO
stops.date_confidence: attested. Inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2009, with continuous observance claimed from 972.
stops.campa: Every third of February the relics leave the treasury and go through the old city behind clergy in medieval vestments, with the parish banners and the doves released in front of the church on the Stradun. In 2009 UNESCO inscribes the festivity on the list of the intangible heritage of humanity, which is the modern world's way of saying what Ragusa said in 972. A thousand and thirty-seven consecutive years is the claim entered on the file, and the city has kept the day through the republic, the earthquake, three empires and a siege.
suggested_refs: UNESCO Representative List, 'Festivity of Saint Blaise, the patron of Dubrovnik' (2009)

stops.name: Goreme, the company painted in the rock
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Goreme rock churches preserve some of the earliest images of Christopher as an armoured soldier martyr. The dating is broad, and no figure at Goreme is identified as Blaise in the reviewed material.
stops.campa: In the tufa churches of Goreme, two hundred kilometres from Sebastea, painters cut and colour the soldier martyrs into the rock, Christopher in armour among them, in some of the earliest surviving images of him anywhere. Cappadocia is transmitting the company visually while northern Europe has barely heard of it. The saints who will be assembled centuries later in a Franconian chapel are already neighbours here, in a valley of caves, in the province next to the one where Blaise was killed.
suggested_refs: The painted rock churches of the Goreme valley, Cappadocia

stops.name: Cologne and the Rhineland, the helpers in need
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Nothelfer devotion originates in the fourteenth century, first in the Rhineland, during the Black Death. The Cologne pin stands for the region; no single founding church is identified in the sources.
stops.campa: The plague comes up the Rhine and the parishes answer it by pooling their intercessors. Fourteen saints, each with a named affliction, are prayed to as one company: the Nothelfer, the helpers in need. Blaise's department is the throat and suffocation, which in a plague year is not a minor one. He is picked for the thing he did to one choking child on a road in Armenia, and now the whole Rhineland is asking him to do it wholesale. Most of the fourteen died in the eastern provinces, a thousand years earlier, and none of them ever saw the river now calling on them.
suggested_refs: The Nothelfer devotion of the Rhineland during the Black Death

stops.name: Franconia, the fourteen fixed as a company
stops.date_confidence: attested. The company is fixed across Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg by about 1400. The Vierzehnheiligen basilica itself is eighteenth century and postdates the devotion by four hundred years.
stops.campa: By about 1400 the list has stopped moving: Acacius, Barbara, Blaise, Catherine, Christopher, Cyriacus, Denis, Erasmus, Eustace, George, Giles, Margaret, Pantaleon, Vitus, kept together at Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg. The atlas already carries the company as one traveler and several of its members singly. Blaise stands third from the left in most of the altarpieces, mitred, holding the comb, sometimes with the two candles crossed under a stranger's chin.
suggested_refs: The Franconian altarpieces of the Vierzehn Nothelfer, c. 1400

segments.name: The Comb, the Candles and the Wool

stops.name: Rome, San Biagio della Pagnotta
stops.date_confidence: attested. The church is first recorded in 1072 and rebuilt under Alexander II.
stops.campa: A church of San Biagio stands on the ground that will become the Via Giulia, first recorded in 1072 and rebuilt under Alexander the Second. Its byname is the Pagnotta, the small loaf, from the blessed bread handed out to the poor at the door on his feast day. Rome takes him late and domesticates him fast: the eastern hieromartyr becomes the parish that gives out bread. The loaves are blessed on the third of February along with the candles, and both go out of the same door.
suggested_refs: San Biagio della Pagnotta on the Via Giulia, Rome

stops.name: Saint-Blaise, a village on Lake Neuchatel
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia gives 1209 for the mention as Sanctus Blasus, the settlement having been recorded as Arins in 1011. Coordinates corrected from a pin about 4 km south, short of the village.
stops.campa: A settlement above the eastern end of Lake Neuchatel, called Arins in 1011, is recorded in 1209 as Sanctus Blasus, and keeps that name afterwards. The dedication swallows the older toponym whole. There is no relic here and no local legend of a visit; there is a parish under his patronage and a village that has answered to his name for eight hundred years, in a country he never heard of, in a language that did not exist when he died. The name outruns the relics: the cult travels as a word before it travels as a bone.
suggested_refs: The commune of Saint-Blaise, canton of Neuchatel, first named Sanctus Blasus in 1209

stops.name: St Blazey, the Cornish town that takes his name
stops.date_confidence: attested. The church was built between 1440 and 1445, replacing one mentioned in 1294, and the town holds a procession and service on 3 February. Coordinates corrected from a pin 2.5 km north, near Luxulyan.
stops.campa: At the head of a tidal creek in Cornwall a church of St Blaise is mentioned in 1294 and rebuilt between 1440 and 1445, and the town around it answers to St Blazey. The parish keeps his procession and service every third of February. Here he is asked for toothache, sore throats and the diseases of cattle, which is the unmercenary physician's original job description arriving intact at the far western edge of Europe, eleven hundred years and four thousand kilometres from Sebastea.
suggested_refs: The parish church of St Blaise at St Blazey, Cornwall, built 1440 to 1445

stops.name: Bromley, the well in the bishop's park
stops.date_confidence: contested. Wikipedia's Bromley article confirms that pilgrims came to St Blaise's Well in the grounds of the bishop's palace; it was a chalybeate medicinal spring drawing pilgrims for indulgences, and no reachable source ties it to the wool combers. The date is a placeholder for a medieval usage of unrecorded start.
stops.campa: In the grounds of the bishop of Rochester's palace at Bromley a chalybeate spring runs under his name, and pilgrims come to it for the water and for the indulgence attached to the visit. The well was lost, forgotten, and found again in the nineteenth century when the estate was being landscaped. The wool combers, who claimed him almost everywhere else in England, are nowhere in its documented history. The well belongs to the older and simpler trade of the healing spring.
suggested_refs: St Blaise's Well in the grounds of the former Bishop's Palace, Bromley

stops.name: Rome, the Roman Ritual and the crossed candles
stops.date_confidence: attested for the formula as printed in the Roman Ritual and quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia. Parish practice of the throat blessing is documented from the later Middle Ages and its first appearance is not recorded; 1614 is the date of the Rituale Romanum, not of the custom.
stops.campa: Two candles are blessed at Candlemas, tied in a cross, and held to the throat of each person who comes up. May God, at the intercession of Saint Blaise, deliver you from ailments of the throat and from every other evil. The gesture is the widow's two candles and the choking boy folded into a single motion lasting four seconds. Few rites in the Roman books work this way, with a saint's biography performed on the body of the faithful rather than recited at them.
stops.quote: Per intercessionem S. Blasii liberet te Deus a malo gutteris et a quovis alio malo.
stops.quote_source: Roman Ritual, Blessing of St. Blaise, Latin formula as quoted in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), s.v. 'St Blaise', newadvent.org/cathen/02592a.htm
suggested_refs: The Blessing of Throats in the Rituale Romanum, kept on and near 3 February

stops.name: Bradford, Bishop Blaize and the wool combers
stops.date_confidence: attested as an early modern to nineteenth century phenomenon at Bradford and Norwich. The medieval English wool comber cult often dated to 1200 is unsupported in reachable sources and that anchor is dropped.
stops.campa: The wool towns of England hold septennial processions for Bishop Blaize: a man in bishop's costume rides at the head, followed by combers in wigs of combed wool, then shepherds, dyers and apprentices carrying their tools, a whole trade walking behind a fourth-century Armenian because a Latin legend said his executioners used their instrument. Bradford's is the famous one, and it runs into the nineteenth century, until combing goes into machines and the machines have no patron.
suggested_refs: The Bishop Blaize processions of Bradford and Norwich, eighteenth and nineteenth centuries

stops.name: Rome, the Armenians given his church
stops.date_confidence: attested. Gregory XVI grants San Biagio della Pagnotta to the Armenian community of Rome as their national church in 1836.
stops.campa: Gregory the Sixteenth gives San Biagio della Pagnotta to the Armenians of Rome as their national church. Fifteen hundred years after a bishop of Lesser Armenia was beheaded in his own city, the Armenian diaspora in the Latin capital is housed under his name, in a building whose byname is a loaf of bread. Nobody planned the circuit. The dedication was made in the eleventh century by Romans who wanted a healer, and the Armenians walked into it eight centuries later.
suggested_refs: San Biagio della Pagnotta as the Armenian national church of Rome, from 1836

stops.name: Sivas, the see with no grave
stops.date_confidence: the Catholic Encyclopedia's own verdict on the Acts, published 1913. What the same article leaves standing is the name, the see at Sebastea, and a martyrdom under Licinius about 316.
stops.campa: The Catholic Encyclopedia, cataloguing its own saints, states the position without softening it: everything in the Acts is legendary and has no claim to historical worth. What survives the sentence is a name, a see at Sebastea, a beheading under Licinius, and a court physician writing two centuries afterwards that you should call on Blaise when something is stuck in a throat. On that footing the wool towns, the crowned skull, the manna, the crossed candles and a Cornish parish were all built.
stops.quote: All the particulars concerning his life and martyrdom which are found in the Acts are purely legendary and have no claim to historical worth.
suggested_refs: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St Blaise, newadvent.org/cathen/02592a.htm
sources: Hippolyte Delehaye, The Legends of the Saints
